patterns: Title formulas dominate: "The Rise and Fall of X", "How X Lost Everything", "Why X Is Failing", "The Untold Story of X", "How X Became a $___ Empire".
Cold opens start at the most dramatic moment (the collapse, the lawsuit, the billion-dollar mistake), then rewind: "To understand how, we need to go back to 1987…".
Winners run 10–25 minutes. Mid-length (8–14 min) versions of big stories outperform their channel average because they get to the point that longer channels pad out.
Visuals are archive photos and news clips, logo and product shots, simple animated maps, stock-price and revenue charts, and kinetic text. Almost nobody shows a face.
Thumbnails: one recognisable logo or product, 1–3 words max ("BANKRUPT", "$0", "IT'S OVER"), a red arrow or crack, high contrast on a dark background.
The human angle wins. Videos built around one founder's bet or one fatal decision get more comments than pure corporate timelines.
Consistent series branding (same intro sting, same chapter cards) builds binge sessions. Top channels link the next story in the outro.
Evergreen giants (Blockbuster, Nokia, Kodak, Toys R Us) are saturated with versions from big channels. New angles or lesser-known giants are the gap.

pillars.name: The Fall
pillars.why: Collapse stories (rise and fall, bankruptcy, scandal) are the most-searched format in the niche and drive the highest views per sub.

pillars.name: The Build
pillars.why: Origin stories of brands people use every day (IKEA, Zara, Red Bull, Nintendo) bring evergreen search traffic and are brand-safe for advertisers, which means higher RPM.

pillars.name: The Bet
pillars.why: One decision that made or broke a company (Netflix killing DVDs, Apple betting on the iPhone). A tight 8–10 minute story with a clear tension arc.

pillars.name: The Comeback
pillars.why: Companies that broke and rebuilt (Lego 2004, Marvel 1996, Apple 1997). Uplifting, under-served compared with collapse stories, and strong for retention.

summary:
No YouTube API data is attached yet (the channel is not connected), so this is based on web research and a review of the leading business-story channels (Company Man, MagnatesMedia, Modern MBA, ColdFusion, Logically Answered).

What works: narrated documentary storytelling about famous companies, told as a drama with a cold open at the moment of crisis. The audience is curious adults, and advertisers pay well for them. Public estimates put business and education RPM around $6–15, versus $2–4 for anime or gaming. Titles follow a few proven formulas (Rise and Fall, How X Lost Everything, Why X Is Failing), and thumbnails are one logo plus one or two shocking words.

What is saturated: the obvious US collapses (Blockbuster, Toys R Us, Sears) have dozens of versions with millions of views. Competing head-on needs a fresh angle ("the one decision that killed Blockbuster") rather than another full timeline.

The gap for Built & Broken: (1) tight 8–10 minute stories where competitors run 25, (2) non-US giants and recent collapses that have fewer versions (Nokia, Wirecard, Evergrande, Kodak inventing the digital camera), (3) the under-served Comeback and Bet formats, and (4) a strong series identity so viewers binge. Connect the YouTube channel to replace this with real view and views-per-subscriber data.
